chapter: Part Two: theaters and the Chicago scene
title: Was there a Chicago style?
summary: Wilson sees little difference; Chicago tempos faster and harder.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: That was nice. Was there a certain way of playing in Chicago? You know, the guys who were born and raised here, like you and Bishop and all the other guys, was there a particular style of playing? You know, like they talk about New Orleans style, they talk about Texas style of playing, New York style, was there a Chicago style of playing?

Well, yes and no. Because when -- like when I first started playing, most of the musicians I worked with was from New Orleans. And they played that old New Orleans style. And later years, they come -- they started what they called the Chicago style, which I didn't see much difference. All I knew; I was playing music. I never paid much attention to the style.
It seems like the guys from
Chicago, you know, who grew up here and --
Yeah, they started playing a different like -- jazz like.
Yeah, a harder --
Harder, yeah.
Hard and driving.
Well, yeah. New Orleans is more --
But it's still here.
Still here, yeah. Because the New Orleans bands, they're still playing that slow, you know, two-beat thing, easy going.
Well, that's one of the things, the tempos were faster here. Still are.
Yeah, they still are.
Pretty fast tempos here in traditional jazz. And it seems to drive more. Seems to be hotter, as they say.
Yeah.
I know a lot of the comments about the Earl Hines band, particularly from Stanley Dance, is that they had fire, and the rhythm was, you know, hard, throbbing, forthright.
That's right.
Sort of like the city.
Yeah.
You come by, it hits you in the head.
(Laughter.)
